clue.text: 1 down type of fish stick

definitions.note: the saying 'as plain as a pikestaff'

blocks.note: a staff is a walking stick

explanation.surface: A fish stick, the frozen breaded kind, of a rather unremarkable sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down is PLAIN, and the English idiom is 'as plain as a pikestaff', so the answer is the proverbial plain thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'plain as a pikestaff' makes this pole the stock example of something obvious and unadorned.

clue.text: Homely type of country

blocks.note: first meaning: unattractive, in the American sense

explanation.walkthrough: In American English 'homely' means unattractive rather than cosy.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means unattractive or unadorned, and the noun names a broad expanse of flat land.

clue.text: In contact like balls on a gate

blocks.note: first meaning: in snooker or billiards, balls touching each other are said to do this
second meaning: a type of country gate swinging in a small enclosure, letting one person through at a time

explanation.surface: Two balls resting against each other on top of a gatepost.
explanation.walkthrough: A kissing gate is a small British field gate that swings within a U-shaped enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Snooker players call touching balls by this term, and the same word names a common style of countryside gate.

clue.text: Like following like?

blocks.note: surface reading: one similar thing coming after another
setter's reading: a word meaning 'of that kind', and the word that 'like' follows in a familiar compound

explanation.walkthrough: The answer means 'like' (of that kind), and is the word that 'like' follows in the compound 'suchlike'.
explanation.definitionFit: As a determiner it means of that sort or similar, a close synonym for the adjective like.

clue.text: Not returning by the main road?

blocks.note: first meaning: gone and not coming back, absent
second meaning: an A-road is a main road in Britain, so travelling the A way

explanation.walkthrough: British main roads are numbered A-roads, so 'the main road' can be 'the A way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has gone off and is absent from home is said to be gone in this sense.

clue.text: Strike a child - infant - not 1 down

blocks.note: to lam is to beat or thrash

explanation.surface: An order to hit a child, a mere baby, with a plea that it not be done plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two letters of the baby word are dropped, unsignalled, before the strike and the child go inside; 1 down is PLAIN, so 'not plain' defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Showy, ostentatious flair is the opposite of something simple and unadorned.

clue.text: Shortly two to three sightless rodents may have us in stitches

indicators.note: said shortly, each word is clipped down to an abbreviated form

blocks.note: two's company, and company is abbreviated CO
the three blind mice of the nursery rhyme, with mice cut short

explanation.surface: A nursery-rhyme scene of blind mice somehow keeping us laughing.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'two's company, three's a crowd' turns two into company; 'Three Blind Mice' is the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian or funny performer is someone whose jokes can leave an audience helpless with laughter.

clue.text: Plan to avail oneself again of liqueur

blocks.note: a chart is a map or plan

explanation.surface: A scheme to have another go at a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A green or yellow herbal spirit made by Carthusian monks in France, named for their monastery.

clue.text: University city raising food - mutton

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it so it reads from the bottom up

blocks.note: mutton is sheep meat, and a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A university town busy rearing sheep for meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in Hesse, Germany, home to one of the oldest Protestant universities in the world.

clue.text: Pet (male) to doctor - one left in city building

explanation.surface: Taking a tomcat to the vet and leaving one behind in town.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain this great church traditionally confers city status, so it is the defining building of a city.

clue.text: Disappointed or ill - terminally, if it's 12's?

blocks.note: first meaning: a British football cliché for being bitterly let down
second meaning: 12 is John Cleese, whose Monty Python sketch features a dead parrot, a bird beyond ill

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is British slang for gutted; in the Dead Parrot sketch Cleese returns a parrot that is very much deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom expresses dismay after a defeat, and Cleese's famous bird is literally sick to the point of death.

clue.text: It's capitally struck from 21

indicators.note: made from another entry, its letters reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Something that has been struck excellently, taken from another answer.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'hit the nail on the head' is the idiom: capitally means on the head, from Latin caput.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter drives this metal spike home by hammering squarely on its flat top.

clue.text: It's hard to understand a goody getting right into evil behaviour

indicators.note: something getting into a thing is going inside it, entering it

blocks.note: a saint, abbreviated ST, is a model of goodness

explanation.surface: A puzzle of why a good person would fall into bad ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes ideas so obscure and recondite that few can grasp them.

clue.text: French setter keeping various echelons for hotelier Basil

indicators.note: various suggests a varied, mixed-up order of letters
keeping something means holding it inside

blocks.note: the setter is 'I', which is je in French

explanation.surface: A French dog keeping assorted ranks of staff in line for a hotel owner.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter is also a dog breed, but in crosswords 'setter' means 'I'. Basil Fawlty runs the hotel in the sitcom Fawlty Towers.
explanation.definitionFit: This actor co-wrote and starred as the manic hotel owner in the BBC sitcom Fawlty Towers.

clue.text: Don't let a lot of Danish money be put among the British: I might grab it

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the end is lost
to put a thing among others is to place it in their midst

explanation.surface: A warning to protect Danish cash in Britain from someone who might snatch it.
explanation.walkthrough: Denmark's currency is the krone, of which only the first three letters are used. The 'I' in the definition is the answer speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief who holds up a financial institution would grab the money, the 'it' of the clue.

clue.text: Walker on island railway has joined the army

definitions.note: a description of the noun, a soldier

blocks.note: a leg is what one walks with

explanation.surface: A hiker on a Scottish island's railway who has enlisted.
explanation.walkthrough: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier of a Roman legion, or of the Foreign Legion, is someone who enlisted in an army.

clue.text: Labour MP gets in: then there's a shortage of pigment

indicators.note: a person who gets in is entering and so ends up inside

explanation.surface: Once a Labour member is elected, some resource runs short.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine black soot collected from burning oil, used as a colouring in ink and paint.

clue.text: Composer of large variation

indicators.note: a variation is an altered version, so the order is changed

explanation.surface: A composer known for a large-scale set of variations.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'variation' nods to this composer's famous Enigma Variations.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edward, the English writer of the Enigma Variations and Pomp and Circumstance marches.

clue.text: Fool dressed for the cold, say?

indicators.note: say means the words are to be spoken and judged by ear

blocks.note: wearing extra clothes, with more on

explanation.surface: Someone foolish enough to be all bundled up against the chill.
explanation.definitionFit: An insult for a stupid person, a dolt or idiot.

clue.text: Girl with American friend, one may gather

explanation.surface: A girl and her American pal, one of whom may collect something.
explanation.walkthrough: Herrick's poem opens 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may'.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous line of verse urges young people to pick these flowers while they can.

clue.text: Vagrant given silk: it's lymphatically wrong

indicators.note: a vagrant wanders about, so the letters stray from their order

explanation.surface: A tramp made a QC (taking silk) when something is wrong with him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vagrant' looks like the person given silk, but it is the anagram signal. Taking silk means becoming a senior British barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrofula, a tuberculous swelling of the lymph glands, was once thought curable by a monarch's touch.

clue.text: Article in house or pod

indicators.note: in places one item inside another

blocks.note: a villa is a large house

explanation.surface: An item found either in a house or in a pod.
explanation.definitionFit: The flavouring comes from the long seed case of a climbing orchid, sold as a pod.

clue.text: Essex men

blocks.note: two men's names, Basil and Don

explanation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London; 'Essex man' is a British stereotype of a brash voter there.
explanation.definitionFit: A new town in the English county east of London, a byword for the county's voters.

clue.text: 1-0 for the dyeing moments?

blocks.note: zero, as in a football score

explanation.surface: A one-nil scoreline in the dying minutes of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dyeing' puns on the dying moments of a game, where a 1-0 score is decided.
explanation.definitionFit: The indigo shrub is a plant source of blue colouring used for staining cloth.

clue.text: It doesn't say who wrote the song  "Keep right on _____ " - no, stop here!

blocks.note: surface padding that sets up the uncredited song
a lay is a song or ballad
the credit word naming a composer
surface padding: the song's title, which goes on 'to the end of the road'

explanation.surface: A song whose writer goes uncredited, about pressing on to the end of the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is Harry Lauder's 'Keep Right On to the End of the Road'; a lay-by is a British roadside parking bay.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside parking bay in Britain where drivers pull off the carriageway and halt.

clue.text: Careful not to turn head, or it'll go crooked

indicators.note: to turn the head round puts its front letters back to front

explanation.surface: Be cautious about swivelling your head, or something will go askew.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first two letters of the answer and you get a word meaning crooked, so turning its head makes it go crooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Cautious and watchful, guarded against danger.

clue.text: My performance is of a student - at a matinee?

explanation.surface: A student actor boasting of a performance at an afternoon show.
explanation.walkthrough: A matinee idol is a handsome star adored by audiences.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart-throb actor of stage or screen, worshipped by fans at afternoon shows.

clue.text: Illustrator to come from sale and buy cover for topless old man

indicators.note: letters that come from other words are remade into something new
without a top means the first letter is gone
to act as cover for something is to wrap around it

explanation.surface: An artist emerging from trading, buying a hat for an old man with no hair.
explanation.walkthrough: A greybeard is an old man; 'cover for' tells you the rearranged letters wrap around what is left of him.
explanation.definitionFit: The English artist of the 1890s known for black ink drawings for Wilde's Salome.

clue.text: Some rice dish to steady the ship

indicators.note: only some of the dish is wanted, its end lopped off

blocks.note: an Anglo-Indian dish of rice, fish and eggs

explanation.surface: A helping of rice served to keep the crew on an even keel.
explanation.definitionFit: A small anchor used to hold or warp a vessel into position.

clue.text: Senior blues

blocks.note: surface reading: elderly people feeling down, or veteran blues musicians
setter's reading: the senior service of Britain's armed forces, whose uniform is dark blue

explanation.walkthrough: Britain's navy is nicknamed the Senior Service as the oldest of its armed forces, and navy blue is named after its uniforms.
explanation.definitionFit: The oldest of the British armed services, clad in dark blue, is called the Senior Service.
